lessons.title: Same Size or Not
lessons.concept: Equal Parts as the Condition for a Fraction

play.targetObjective: Decide whether a whole has been cut into equal parts.
stepByStep: Look along the parts, not at how many there are.
Compare two of them at a time.
If any two are different sizes, it is not a fair split.
A fraction only means something when every part is the same.
play.kidTip: Four pieces is not quarters unless all four are the same size.
play.audioPrompt: Are all the parts the same size?

prompts.default: Are all the parts the same size?

lessons.title: One of Them
lessons.concept: Naming One of a Number of Equal Parts

play.targetObjective: Name one part of a whole cut into equal parts.
stepByStep: Count how many equal parts the whole is cut into.
That number goes underneath.
One part is shaded, so a one goes on top.
One of four equal parts is one quarter.
play.kidTip: The number underneath tells you how many pieces the whole was cut into — not how big they are.
play.audioPrompt: One part is shaded. What is it called?

lessons.title: Half of What?
lessons.concept: A Fraction as a Quantity Only Once the Whole Is Named

play.targetObjective: Recognise that the same fraction of different wholes is different amounts.
stepByStep: Check the fraction shaded on each one. They are the same.
Now look at how big the two wholes are.
The same fraction of a bigger whole is a bigger amount.
A fraction on its own is not an amount until you say what it is a fraction of.
play.kidTip: Half a biscuit and half a cake are both a half. They are not both the same amount of food.
play.audioPrompt: Both have the same fraction shaded. Which is more?

lessons.title: Three of Those
lessons.concept: Building a Fraction from Copies of Its Unit Fraction

play.targetObjective: Make a fraction by shading that many copies of one part.
stepByStep: Look at how many parts the whole is cut into.
Each one of them is one of those parts.
Shade them one at a time, counting as you go.
Three quarters is three lots of one quarter. It is one number, not two.
play.kidTip: Every fraction is just so many copies of one piece.
play.audioPrompt: Shade that many of the parts, one at a time.

lessons.title: Writing It Down
lessons.concept: Reading a Picture as a Fraction

play.targetObjective: Write the fraction a picture shows.
stepByStep: Count the shaded parts.
Count all the parts.
The shaded ones go on top; all of them go underneath.
Read it out loud to check it sounds right.
play.kidTip: If you put them the other way up you have written something bigger than the whole.
play.audioPrompt: Count the shaded parts, then count all of them.

lessons.title: A Fraction of a Group
lessons.concept: Fractions of a Set Rather Than of One Object

play.targetObjective: Find a fraction of a set of objects.
stepByStep: The whole is the whole set, not one of the things in it.
Split the set into as many equal groups as the bottom number says.
Count how many are in one group.
Take as many groups as the top number says.
play.kidTip: A third of twelve marbles is four marbles — the whole is all twelve.
play.audioPrompt: Split the set into equal groups first.

lessons.title: One Jump Along
lessons.concept: Placing a Unit Fraction as a Number

play.targetObjective: Put a unit fraction in its place on a number line.
stepByStep: Look at how many equal jumps the line is cut into between 0 and 1.
Each jump is one of those parts.
Count one jump from zero.
Stop there. That is where the fraction lives.
play.kidTip: A fraction is not only part of a cake. It is a number with a place of its own.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.

lessons.title: Count the Jumps
lessons.concept: Placing Any Proper Fraction as a Number

play.targetObjective: Put any fraction below one in its place on a number line.
stepByStep: Every jump along the line is one of the bottom number's parts.
The top number tells you how many jumps to take.
Count them from zero, one at a time.
Land on the mark, not between two.
play.kidTip: Top number, that many jumps. Bottom number, how big each jump is.
play.audioPrompt: Count that many jumps from zero.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.

lessons.title: What Is It Standing On?
lessons.concept: Reading a Fraction off a Number Line

play.targetObjective: Name the fraction a marker is sitting on.
stepByStep: Count the jumps from zero up to the marker. That is the top number.
Count all the jumps from 0 to 1. That is the bottom number.
Count jumps, never marks — there is always one more mark than jump.
Read it back and check it sounds smaller than one.
play.kidTip: The commonest slip here is counting the marks. Five marks means four jumps.
play.audioPrompt: Count the jumps from zero to the marker.

prompts.default: What number is the marker on?

lessons.title: Enough to Make One
lessons.concept: A Fraction with the Same Number Top and Bottom

play.targetObjective: Recognise that a fraction can be exactly one whole.
stepByStep: Count the jumps from 0 all the way to 1.
However many that is, that many of those parts make one whole.
So four quarters is one, and eight eighths is one.
Same number top and bottom always means one whole.
play.kidTip: A fraction does not have to be less than one. Some fractions are whole numbers.
play.audioPrompt: How many of those parts make one whole?

lessons.title: Past the One
lessons.concept: Improper Fractions as Numbers Beyond One

play.targetObjective: Place a fraction bigger than one on a number line.
stepByStep: This line carries on past 1.
The jumps are all the same size as before.
Count them from zero and go straight past the 1 without stopping.
A fraction bigger than one is still one number with one place.
play.kidTip: Seven quarters is just seven jumps of a quarter. Nothing stops at one.

prompts.default: Put the marker on the fraction.
